h1: What an SEO tool stack actually costs in India
metaTitle: What an SEO Tool Stack Costs in India
metaDescription: A ₹40,000 in-house salary plus ₹30,000 of tools is not a ₹40,000 decision. Our real stack in rupees per month, and the order we would cut it in.
answer: Our working SEO tool stack costs roughly ₹58,000–₹67,000 a month: one keyword and link suite, two extra seats, a crawler licence, a rank tracker, a second suite for cross-checking, and reporting. Across a live roster that's ₹6,000–₹9,000 per client. Almost all of it is priced in dollars, so the bill moves without asking.
takeaways: Tools are the line that goes missing from every in-house-versus-agency comparison, because salaries are quoted in rupees and tools are quoted in dollars.
A single-seat working stack is **₹19,000–₹33,000/mo**. A ₹40,000 hire is therefore a ₹65,000-plus decision before employer costs.
We could halve our bill in three cuts. The first two cost almost nothing; the third costs about a day a week of delivery.
**The free Google stack is not a consolation prize.** It's the only true record of your own queries, clicks and links, and paid tools mainly exist to show you everyone else's.
Forex is a live line item. The reference rate moved enough this year that a stack budgeted in January is not the stack you're paying for now.

sections.h2: Our monthly tool bill, line by line
body: We publish our prices, so publishing what sits behind them is the same argument continued. This is the shape of our tooling spend for a team of four, at list prices, converted honestly.

The conversion matters as much as the list price. The RBI reference rate was **₹95.73** to the dollar on the day we costed this, and most Indian cards add 2–3.5% on a foreign transaction, so we've landed everything at roughly **₹98.60**. Your number will differ by the day and by the card.

callout.body: Every paid row above is billed in dollars. A five-rupee move in the exchange rate changes this stack by about ₹3,000 a month, and nobody sends you a notice. If you're building an in-house budget, add a forex contingency or expect to explain a variance you didn't cause.

sections.h2: What each line is load-bearing for, and what is habit
body: Not every row above survives honest scrutiny, and pretending otherwise would make this page an advert rather than a cost breakdown. Two of the six are genuinely irreplaceable, two are operational, and two are convenience we could defend at a client's expense but shouldn't.
bullets: **The backlink index is the real product.** Somebody has to crawl the web continuously and store what links to what. That's expensive to run, which is why it's expensive to rent, and it's the one thing you cannot approximate for free at competitor scale.
**The crawler licence is load-bearing and cheap.** ₹2,000 a month to audit a 6,000-page site properly is the best value in the stack, and it's the last thing we'd give up.

**Extra seats are operational, not optional.** One login shared by three people means rate limits, credits exhausted by the third week, and somebody queueing to pull your data. It looks like a saving on the invoice and isn't.

**The rank tracker is half habit.** Search Console already reports average position for every query you appear on. The tracker adds daily granularity by city and device — useful for local work, largely decorative for a national B2B account.

**The second suite is habit.** Two keyword databases disagree constantly, especially on Hindi and Hinglish volume, and [Ahrefs and Semrush are strong at different jobs](/compare/ahrefs-vs-semrush). It's still a comfort purchase, and we'd say so before we'd defend it.

sections.h2: The cut order, if the budget has to halve
body: Every founder building an in-house function asks the same question in a different order: not what should I buy, but what can I drop. So here's the sequence we'd actually follow, and what each cut costs in capability rather than in rupees.
Three cuts take our bill from about ₹58,000 to roughly ₹27,000. The first two are cheap. The third is where delivery genuinely slows.

callout.title: The cut we'd make before any of these
callout.body: If the budget is genuinely tight, cut the number of sites before you cut the stack. One site done properly with a full toolkit beats three done blind, and the tools are close to a fixed cost while the work is not.

sections.h2: What free actually covers, and exactly where it stops
body: The honest position — which costs us money to state — is that for a single Indian site in its first six months, the correct tool budget is zero. Almost everything a small site needs is already sitting in an account you haven't finished setting up.

[Search Console is free, and it also shows you which sites link to yours](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9128668), which is the fact most people are surprised by. It is the only authoritative record of your own queries, clicks and average position, and no paid tool has access to it.
bullets: **Your own query data** — Search Console, free, complete for your property, and better than any tracker's estimate of the same thing.
**Your own backlinks** — Search Console's Links report, plus the free webmaster tier most link vendors offer for domains you verify.
**Real-user speed data** — the Chrome UX Report feeds PageSpeed Insights, and it's the same field data Google uses. Free, and more relevant than a lab score.

**Analytics and reporting** — GA4 and Looker Studio, at zero, cover almost every client report we build. Configuring them well matters far more than paying for an alternative, which is why [filtering bot traffic out of GA4](/answers/how-to-filter-bot-traffic-in-ga4) is worth an afternoon.
**A second search engine's view** — Bing Webmaster Tools gives free keyword and audit data on a different index. Underused because it isn't Google.

subs.h3: The three things free genuinely cannot do
bullets: **Competitor backlinks at depth.** Search Console shows your links, never theirs. This is the gap that eventually justifies a subscription and nothing else quite does.
**Crawling a large site.** Free crawler tiers stop at 500 URLs, which covers a lot of Indian SME sites entirely and no ecommerce catalogue at all.

**Analysis at multi-client scale.** Once you're across several properties and want long histories in one place, the interface stops being the right tool — Search Console's own bulk export to BigQuery exists precisely for that, and it is also free apart from what BigQuery charges.

body: Here is the reason this page exists. Every in-house-versus-agency comparison on the internet puts a salary in one column and a retainer in the other, and quietly omits the tools — because salaries are quoted in rupees and tools are quoted in dollars, so they end up in different spreadsheets.
Put them in the same column and the maths changes shape. A ₹40,000-a-month hire is not a ₹40,000-a-month decision.

bullets: This isn't an argument that in-house is wrong. It's an argument that ₹40,000 is the wrong number to put against ₹75,000 — the honest comparison is ₹65,000-plus against ₹75,000, and the decision then turns on range versus context rather than on price.

A senior hire changes the picture again, in the other direction. [What it costs to hire SEO talent in India](/journal/what-it-costs-to-hire-seo-talent-in-india) has the salary bands; [the full year-one comparison is here](/compare/agency-vs-in-house).

Tools are close to a fixed cost, so they get cheaper per unit as you do more. That's the one structural advantage a larger agency has over a small in-house team, and we'll concede it without argument.
The hybrid usually wins: one in-house owner of organic, plus an agency for range. The tool bill sits on our side of that arrangement, which is part of why it's cheaper than it looks.

sections.h2: Three ways an agency's tool bill quietly becomes your problem
body: Tooling is a cost of doing our job, not a cost of being your client. Most of the time that's how it's treated. These are the three arrangements where it stops being true, all of them visible in a proposal if you know to look, and none of them a scandal.
numbered: **Tools re-invoiced to you with a handling fee.** Legitimate for enterprise licences bought in your name; a second fee when it's the agency's own stack. Ask whether tools are inside the retainer or on top, and get the answer in writing.

**The whole stack in the agency's name.** Rank tracking history, crawl archives and audit records live in their account. At exit you keep the site and lose the baseline — which is the number you were being measured against. Ask what tool data comes with you when you leave.

**Tools bought instead of hours.** A ₹25,000 stack produces far more findings than one person can act on. If the reporting is getting richer while the shipped work is flat, you're paying for a better description of the problem. [Where the retainer money actually goes](/journal/where-your-seo-retainer-money-actually-goes) puts tools at 8–12% of a fee — if it feels like more than that, something else has gone quiet.

callout.title: The question that produces the useful pause
callout.body: "Which tools do you pay for, and how many seats?" It's a boring question with a fast answer at a well-run firm. A vague one means either a shared login and a rate limit with your name on it, or a stack thinner than the proposal implies.

faqs.q: What does an SEO tool stack cost per month in India?
faqs.a: A single-seat working stack runs ₹19,000–₹33,000 a month: one keyword and link suite, a crawler licence and a rank tracker. A small agency team lands at ₹58,000–₹67,000 once you add seats and a second suite. Almost everything is dollar-priced, so the rupee figure moves with the exchange rate.

faqs.q: Can you do SEO with only free tools?
faqs.a: For a single site in its first six months, genuinely yes. Search Console, GA4, PageSpeed Insights, the Chrome UX Report, Bing Webmaster Tools and a free crawler tier cover most of the job. What free can't do is competitor backlink analysis at depth, crawl past 500 URLs, or track ranks daily by city.

faqs.q: Which SEO tool should I buy first?
faqs.a: A crawler licence, at roughly ₹2,000 a month spread annually. It's the cheapest line in any stack and the one that finds problems you can act on this week. The keyword and link suite comes second, and only once you actually need competitor data rather than your own.

faqs.q: Do agencies include tool costs in the retainer?
faqs.a: Most do, and it's usually 8–12% of the fee. Some re-invoice licences with a handling charge, which is reasonable only when the licence is bought in your name. Ask the question directly before you sign — whether tools sit inside the retainer or on top of it, in writing.

faqs.q: Why are SEO tools so expensive in India?
faqs.a: Because they're priced in dollars for a market with much higher willingness to pay, and nothing about the rupee conversion is discounted. Add a 2–3.5% card markup on foreign transactions and 18% GST as an imported service, and the landed cost is meaningfully above the list price you read on the site.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to hire in-house than to pay an agency, once tools are counted?
faqs.a: Rarely, at the entry level. A ₹40,000 hire plus a ₹19,000–₹33,000 single-seat stack plus 15–25% of employer costs lands at ₹65,000–₹1,20,500 a month against a ₹75,000 retainer that already includes the tools. In-house buys context and availability, not a lower number.
